methods.label: Interpret absolute values as distances
methods.explanation:
The expressions \(|x-2|\) and \(|x-3|\) measure the distances from \(x\) to \(2\) and \(3\) on the number line. Since these fixed points are \(1\) unit apart, consider where \(x\) lies relative to them.

If \(2\le x\le3\), the two distances together make the entire segment from \(2\) to \(3\), so their sum is \(1\). This includes both endpoints, where one distance is zero.

If \(x<2\), its distance to \(3\) alone is greater than \(1\). If \(x>3\), its distance to \(2\) alone is greater than \(1\). Therefore no number outside the interval satisfies the equation.

The solution set is exactly \([2,3]\). A real interval of positive length contains infinitely many numbers, so there are infinitely many solutions. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{E}}\), more than \(3\).
methods.levelReason: Uses elementary number-line distances and addition of segment lengths.

methods.label: Split where the signs change
methods.explanation:
The expressions \(x-2\) and \(x-3\) change sign at \(2\) and \(3\). These values divide all real numbers into three cases, allowing us to remove the absolute-value signs correctly.

For \(x<2\), both expressions are negative, so
\[
|x-2|+|x-3|=(2-x)+(3-x)=5-2x>1.
\]
For \(2\le x\le3\), the first expression is nonnegative and the second is nonpositive, so
\[
|x-2|+|x-3|=(x-2)+(3-x)=1.
\]
For \(x>3\), both expressions are positive, so
\[
|x-2|+|x-3|=(x-2)+(x-3)=2x-5>1.
\]
Thus the equation holds exactly when \(2\le x\le3\), including both endpoints. This interval has positive length and contains infinitely many real numbers. Therefore the answer is \(\boxed{\text{E}}\), more than \(3\).
methods.levelReason: Uses elementary absolute-value rules, combining like terms, and inequality properties.
